Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin

Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts : hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.

This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra

August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties .

Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.

The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.

El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.

The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.

Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.

China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.

Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.

China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies

In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.

To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.

They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.

In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.

Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.

Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains

Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season , and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.

The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.

But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.

"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.

"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results

Elon Musk spent almost $450m (£334m) – more than anyone ever has in an election cycle – to back Republican political candidates in the US midterm races. It was not enough to keep Democrats from a resounding victory .

Among the most striking wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas. Musk spent at least $45m in support of Paxton, according to a BBC analysis of campaign finance data .

Other races where Musk spent millions included Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota. His spending continued into Monday, records show.

By Tuesday night, Musk seemed to admit defeat, joking on X that his "election-interfering space lasers didn't work."

LIVE UPDATES: All the latest developments

BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

RESULTS: How America voted in maps and charts

EXPLAINER: Five reasons why Trump did so badly

ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now

REACTION: Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms 'disaster'

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox

The loss this week of so many Republican seats may have significant implications for Musk and his businesses.

SpaceX has gained an estimated , external $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was elected to his second non-consecutive term. Several Democratic lawmakers have said the company's extensive and growing role in government and national security should be investigated , external .

SpaceX's future development of massive data centres is also facing new potential difficulties - as are the data centre developments of other tech companies.

In Georgia for instance, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the just elected Democratic governor ran in-part on limiting the rapid rise of the massive buildings , as well as the huge tax breaks tech companies usually get to build them.

A number of other politicians ran on limiting data centres and dozens of state measures to limit their development passed on Tuesday , external .

Data centres are sprawling buildings that house stacks of computing hardware. Tech and artificial intelligence (AI) companies use them to run online platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Musk's X and his AI company xAI.

Musk posted to X on Tuesday that his previously floated idea to somehow build data centres in space was "looking pretty appealing right now."

Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly

Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.

Tech companies involved in AI may be in for a tougher government scrutiny and potential regulation with Democrats in power, though any legislation would need Trump's approval.

James Flintoft, head of investment solutions at AJ Bell, pointed to Musk's unsuccessful spending on Republican candidates and the scale of wins by Democrats as bringing in a "period of uncertainty for investors as they assess whether tech companies are set to face greater regulation."

Senator Ed Markey on Wednesday responded on X to a person asking if major tech industry executives would be the target of investigations, saying: "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."

Tech stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning. Yet, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively.

By Wednesday, Musk had stopped posting to X about politics and was instead posting in praise of GrokBot, an AI chatbot produced by xAI. It was a stark contrast to the 2025 election, when Musk would post to X sometimes hundreds of times in a day about politics.

He also unpinned a post that had been saved to the top of his X profile since last week that explained his "concern" with Democratic politicians winning more midterm races.

Those concerns included the idea that the US could welcome more immigrants, make Washington DC and Puerto Rico individual states, and expand the number of justices on the Supreme Court.

Another post telling his 241 million X followers to "Vote red today!" appeared on Wednesday to have been deleted from Musk's profile.

The BBC has contacted SpaceX for comment about Musk's spending and posts.

While Musk spent millions of dollars backing Republican candidates in multiple US states, a lot of his political focus seemed to be on Texas.

In recent years, Musk made the state the corporate headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX, both of which still have large operations in California where they were founded.

"There is something deeply wrong with Talarico", Musk posted to X in October.

Talarico posted in response: "There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator."

Not all billionaires in the US shared Musk's preference for Republicans.

Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire and the founder of LinkedIn who is a major donor to Democrats, hailed the results of Tuesday's elections as an event that "blew the doors off our expectations."

"These elections were an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies," Hoffman wrote on X and on LinkedIn. "While people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."

Kellogg's has told the BBC the "snap, crackle and pop" sound made by its Rice Krispies may be noticeably quieter after an uproar over the cereal giant's recipe change.

Rice Krispies and Coco Pops are no longer being made with whole rice grains, with the tiny toasted puffs being made using corn flour and rice flour instead.

A Kellogg's spokesperson said retaining the iconic sound had been a "huge focus" when designing the new recipe, but that customers "might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".

The firm was responding to complaints online that the taste of the breakfast staples had changed, with some fans adding they missed the "pop" sound.

Kellogg's said it had adapted the recipes due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies of some grains and cereals.

The cereal giant said the new versions had been "carefully assessed for taste, appearance and texture", but some shoppers said their children would no longer eat them.

Some expressed dismay that the taste and texture were "totally different" and dubbed the change "grim" and "disgusting".

"There's no snap, crackle and pop in these," a parent named Dani wrote on TikTok. "My toddler won't eat them."

Lauren, also posting on TikTok, added that she had been eating Rice Krispies every day for breakfast "for years and years".

"I had a bowl of the new recipe and you can immediately tell the difference," she said. "They don't have the snapping sound when you put in the milk."

Jessicake meanwhile said they tasted "weird and stale".

The "Snap, Crackle and Pop" - made when milk is added to the puffed rice - has been a centrepiece of the brand's marketing since the 1950s.

Kellogg's insisted the snap, crackle and pop is "still there, but consumers might notice that the sound may be quieter and not as instant as before".

Recipe changes are notoriously difficult for big brands. Chocolate makers are constantly accused of reducing cocoa content in their products and debates rage online over whether ketchup ingredients have changed.

When Scottish fizzy drink Irn Bru cut its sugar content in 2018, fans famously stockpiled crates of the old version .

No changes are being made to Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada, which are owned by a separate company.

Kellogg's said the recipe change in the UK would help "maintain consistent quality" as extreme weather takes a toll on crops and pushes up ingredient prices.

Extreme weather in Spain in 2022 and 2023 in particular had reduced availability of the types of rice the company uses for its breakfast cereals, the company said.

Rice Krispies, launched nearly a century ago, are sold around the world and come in variations such as vanilla and strawberry flavours in some markets alongside the widespread chocolate-flavoured Coco Pops version.

"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration," Kellogg's said.

The firm said it appreciated the customer feedback and would "continue to look at ways to make [its] products even better in the future".

The cereals have already undergone some change, with reductions in salt content in the 1990s and lowered sugar in 2018. The company said Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.

A backlash against processed foods in recent years, especially those low in fibre and high in sugar, has put breakfast cereals generally under the spotlight from healthy eating advocates.

Kellogg's stressed the cereals contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same.

However, the new recipes mean packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning. It also continues to contain barley-malt extract.

Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?

Kellogg's said it has not changed the recipe for any of its other cereals.

Many parts of the world have been affected by droughts, floods and heatwaves this year due to the El Niño weather phenomenon. The weather event is expected to severely affect crop production from South East Asia in particular. The region produces more than a quarter of the world's rice.

The World Meteorological Agency expects the record-breaking El Niño will last until at least 2027.

That will intensify pressure on food manufacturing companies, already looking at ways to source reliable and affordable ingredients.

The original Kellogg company separated into two distinct firms in 2023.

The largest is Kellanova, which focuses on snacks, cereals, noodles and other food products like Eggo, Pringles and Pop-Tarts sold globally. It is now owned by Mars, which makes confectionery and pet food.

The other business, WK Kellogg's, operates in North America and has since been taken over by Italian chocolate giant Ferrero .

Crow shares her admiration for country legend Dolly Parton, who also had Welsh ancestry

American singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow has described her "incredible" links to Wales, revealing that her mother's side of the family was from the country.

Speaking to Bronwen Lewis on BBC Radio Wales , the nine-time Grammy winner recalled visiting Wales for the first time with her parents in about 1990 while touring as a backing singer for Michael Jackson.

Crow, best known for hits including All I Wanna Do and If It Makes You Happy, said she did not know where exactly in Wales her family came from, but expressed a desire to research her heritage further.

"I need to do one of those DNA things," she said.

Crow also discussed the legacy of country music legend Dolly Parton - whose family tree has been traced to Machynlleth in Powys.

Lewis, also a singer-songwriter, shared with Crow that she collaborated on a Welsh language version of the song Jolene with Parton and Parton's niece, Jada Star.

The song was released on 9 October after Parton's death on 25 August 2026 .

Crow said she would love to have her songs translated into Welsh, and called Parton a "wonderful person" and "a singer no-one could compete with".

She said Parton's death had made her reflect on her contribution to the world: "For me, when she passed away, for the next two to three weeks I walked around feeling like am I doing enough to serve humanity?

"Am I doing enough to lift up people in my community?

"Because she was not only masterful at it, but selfless about it."

Crow highlighted Parton's Imagination Library , her literacy programme that sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five, as an example of this philanthropy.

Bronwen Lewis showcases new and classic country music from Wales and the world.

Crow, who was born in Missouri, has worked professionally as a singer for almost 40 years, starting as a backing singer on Jackson's Bad World Tour before releasing her commercially successful debut album Tuesday Night Music Club in 1993.

She has collaborated with several artists including Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, Stevie Nicks and Eric Clapton and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2023.

Cocaine-related deaths overtook heroin for the first time in 2015

The number of deaths from cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade, overtaking those attributed to heroin for the first time.

Cocaine was linked to more than one in five drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025, more than any other single substance, with charities blaming its increased purity and availability.

Meanwhile a record 115 ketamine-linked deaths were registered, almost twice as many as in 2024, according to Office for National Statistics data , external .

The overall rate of drug deaths fell for the first time since 2012. But experts pointed out regional inequality was growing, with the rate of such deaths more than twice as high in the North East as in London.

There were 5,519 drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025 in England and Wales, the equivalent of 92.4 deaths per million people.

Of these, cocaine was mentioned in 1,233 cases - slightly fewer than the previous year but higher than the 1,210 deaths linked to heroin or morphine, which also marked a fall from the previous year's level.

However, deaths linked to opiate and opioid drugs combined were still higher. The ONS also said there was a lag between deaths occurring and being registered.

The fatality rate fell from 93.9 deaths per million people a year earlier, representing the first annual decline since 2012.

In September, National Records of Scotland said drug deaths there had risen by 11% in 2025 on the year before, marking the worst mortality rate in Europe,

In May the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency said drug-related deaths rose by 7.1% between 2021-23 and 2022-24 , external .

Dr James Morgan, who specialises in addiction and mental health at London Metropolitan University, said while there had been a slight decrease in deaths "the numbers remain objectively high", with total drug fatalities in England and Wales roughly doubling since 2012.

"What we are seeing is increasing polarisation and growing inequalities, where the poorest regions are falling behind, and more affluent regions doing better," he said.

The steepest increases were found in formerly industrial areas with high levels of poverty and unemployment dating back to the 1980s, including the North East, Wales, Yorkshire and the Humber, the North West and the East Midlands.

Morgan pointed out that cocaine death figures included not only those who snorted the drug but also users who injected it or smoke crack cocaine in combination with opioids or counterfeit pharmaceutical drugs.

"The small decline in deaths related to cocaine should not be over-interpreted. Most important is that deaths relating to cocaine remain roughly quadruple what they were in 2015 and are now more frequent than deaths relating to heroin or morphine," he said.

Meanwhile, ketamine was referenced in 115 deaths last year - almost double the year before and up from just seven fatalities 10 years earlier.

Morgan said this was down to lower prices and use of the drug becoming normalised. He said there were increasing reports of young people becoming dependent on ketamine and suffering acute health difficulties such as bladder damage.

Anthony Irvin (pictured with sister Nyk) died from drug poisoning in 2025

Mike Trace, CEO of the addiction charity Forward Trust, said drug poisoning deaths remained high because of factors including the proliferation of very strong synthetic opioid drugs called nitazenes .

"We know that increasingly potent drugs like nitazenes are making their way on to the market. We know that established drugs like cocaine are growing in purity which means they come with much higher risks to users," he said.

Nitazenes can be many times more potent than heroin and have been linked to hundreds of UK deaths.

Tom Powell and Nyk Irvin's brother Anthony Irvin died from drug poisoning in Ramsgate in September 2025 at the age of 52.

His siblings believe his death was caused by a supply of drugs being contaminated with synthetic opioids, but say delays in blood testing mean they will never know for sure.

"Today's figures are shocking," Powell said. "We are fighting to wake people up to the scale of the problem."

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE , a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here . To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com .

French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.

"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.

Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.

Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.

But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.

While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.

Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.

Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.

In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.

By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.

According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.

"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.

The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.

Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.

It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.

Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.

"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.

A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.

In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.

But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.

"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.

According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.

Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.

"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.

"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."

Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.

Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.

But no formal attribution has been made.

None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.

But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.

Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

MN202611_1bfw7shcbrj.t: Diplomatic missions from 11 countries are expected to bring their cultures to Kigali for the second edition of the Rwanda Diplomatic Charity Bazaar, showcasing their food, traditions, fashion, music and heritage. The event, scheduled for November 21 at Kigali Conference and Exhibition Village, also known as Camp Kigali, will bring together diplomatic missions, international delegates, cultural practitioners, businesses and the public under the theme “Promoting Cultural Diplomacy and Community Empowerment”. ALSO READ: Diplomats laud cultural exchange at Charity Bazaar fair According to Edison Niyontegereje, president and chief organiser of the bazaar and chief executive of Intercultural Bridge Group CBC (IBG CBC), 11 diplomatic missions had confirmed participation as of October 17, including Angola, Kenya, Russia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Algeria, Gabon, Uganda, Libya, Ghana and Tanzania. “Visitors are expected to explore different cultures through country exhibitions, cultural performances, international cuisine and creative products.” “As the international community increasingly comes to Rwanda, we have been seeing that they don't even have places where they can connect with the local community, with students coming to study here, people coming to do business here, and even diplomatic missions,” he added. The organisers expect more than 5,000 visitors at the event. Beyond cultural displays, the event is also intended to help local artists, artisans and other creative entrepreneurs, including those working with the Agaseke Centre, showcase their products to international audiences and access wider markets. ALSO READ: Inaugural Diplomatic Charity Bazaar targets to empower rural artisans Joe Francis, director of education and culture at IBG CBC, said the event would also connect local creatives with artists and artisans from other countries, allowing them to exchange ideas and learn new approaches. “Through these connections, local artists and artisans can develop new ways of managing their initiatives,” he added. A cultural art auction is also being prepared under the theme “Art, Culture, Humanity”. Organisers plan to feature original works by painters, sculptors and other visual artists. The bazaar follows its inaugural edition, held on November 22, 2025, at Green Hills Academy in Kigali.

Amajyepfo: Abaturage bo mu turere dutandukanye bari baribwe ibikoresho by’ikoranabuhanga mu bihe bitandukanye bishimiye kubisubizwa na Polisi y’u Rwanda, bashimira inzego z’umutekano zabafashije kongera kubona imitungo yabo.

Igikorwa cyo gusubiza ibi bikoresho cyabereye mu karere ka Gisagara.

Polisi ivuga ko ibikorwa byo guhangana n’ubujura bikomeje, harimo no gufata ibikoresho n’amatungo byibwe bigasubizwa ba nyirabyo.

Uwayisenga Aliane wo mu Murenge wa Ngoma, mu Karere ka Huye avuga ko yari yibwe printer n’ibindi bikoresho, ariko akishimira ko yabisubijwe, agashimira Polisi y’u Rwanda yabigizemo uruhare.

Yagize ati: “Ndashimira Polisi y’u Rwanda yafashe ibikoresho byanjye ikabinsubiza. Nishimiye kongera kubona umutungo wanjye nari naribwe.”

Ndagijimana Sylivestre wo mu Murenge wa Huye avuga ko yari yaribwe televiziyo, yishimira ko yayisubijwe nyuma y’uko Polisi y’u Rwanda igize uruhare mu kuyigaruza.

Yagize ati: “Ndashimira Polisi y’u Rwanda yamfashije kongera kubona televiziyo yanjye. Ibi binteye imbaraga zo gufatanya na Polisi mu gukumira ibyaha no gutanga amakuru ku gihe igihe mbonye ibitagenda neza.”

Iradukunda Felisi wo mu Karere ka Huye mu murenge wa Huye na we avuga ko yari yaribwe radiyo na televiziyo, ashimira Polisi y’u Rwanda yabafashije kongera kubona ibikoresho byabo.

Umuvugizi wa Polisi y’u Rwanda mu Ntara y’Amajyepfo, CIP Hassan Kamanzi, avuga ko ibikoresho by’ikoranabuhanga bitandukanye birimo radiyo, televiziyo na telefoni, ndetse n’ibindi byasubijwe ba nyirabyo nyuma yo gufatwa mu bihe bitandukanye.

CIP Hassan Kamanzi avuga ko uretse ibikoresho by’ikoranabuhanga, hari n’amatungo yagiye yibwa hirya no hino agenda afatwa agasubizwa ba nyirayo.

Yagize ati: “Ibikoresho by’ikoranabuhanga bitandukanye birimo amaradiyo, televiziyo na telefoni ndetse n’ibindi byasubijwe ba nyirabyo, byari byaribwe mu bihe bitandukanye. Hari n’amatungo yagiye yibwa agenda afatwa agasubizwa ba nyirayo.”

Yavuze ko ibikorwa byo guhangana n’ubujura bikomeje, ashimangira ko Polisi y’u Rwanda n’izindi nzego zitazihanganira abakora ibikorwa by’ubujura.

Yasabye abakora ubujura kubireka bagakora ibikorwa bibateza imbere, birinda ibikorwa bishobora guhungabanya umutekano w’abandi.

Polisi y’u Rwanda ikomeza gusaba abaturage kugira uruhare mu gukumira ibyaha, batanga amakuru ku gihe ku bikorwa by’ubujura n’ibindi bishobora guhungabanya umutekano.

Belfast Trust took possession of the new maternity hospital in March 2024

Almost £20m in additional costs due to problems at two Belfast Health Trust buildings has been described as "such terrible waste".

Newly-discovered issues with the Belfast maternity hospital could add almost £10m to the project's spiralling costs, while the amount spent on repairs and rehousing patients at the Acute Mental Health facility has now reached £9.4m.

Daniel McCrossan, who chairs the Public Accounts Committee, said: "We can't see such waste, such terrible waste, within our public sector and then still go to London and demand more [money]."

The Department of Health (DoH) said the extra building costs are "disappointing" but it is essential they are "completed and delivered".

The maternity building on the Royal Victoria Hospital (RVH) site is already tens of millions of pounds over budget and more than a decade behind schedule. The new costs mean the project will exceed £100m.

It is understood the latest problem at the maternity hospital has been caused by chemical flushing aimed at dealing with the original issue of bacteria in the water system.

Investigation into new maternity hospital 'a clever ruse' not to answer questions

'Shocking': More delay for ten years overdue £97m maternity hospital

New Belfast maternity hospital could face a further 28-month delay

The flushing process has caused damage to the pipework, with more than 2,200 defective valves needing replaced.

A report seen by the BBC estimates a repair bill of £7.8m, with an option of 24-hour contractor working bringing that close to £10m. Work to replace the valves is now under way.

Stormont's Public Accounts Committee oversees public spending in Northern Ireland.

SDLP MLA McCrossan said "the buck stops with the Department of Health".

"There needs to be some accountability here when it comes to the use, and indeed misuse, of public money where wastage could have been prevented."

McCrossan added that every pound counts because "it is public money".

"There needs to be very clear accountability here and we need a reassurance because we've sought this - when are these facilities going to actually open to benefit the taxpayer whose money has been invested in building it?

"When are patients going to get the benefit out of using these facilities which they're designed for?

"And ultimately, how much more are we going to stick sticking plasters over problems instead of grabbing the bull by the horns and getting these things done?"

The new maternity facility is due to replace the existing Royal Jubilee maternity hospital at the Royal Victoria Hospital, but the opening date remains in doubt because of the ongoing repair issues.

The building was handed over to the Belfast Trust in March 2024, but the discovery of the potentially dangerous pseudomonas bacterium in the water system and other problems has meant the hospital has remained closed.

An investigation by trust managers into the building handover and subsequent water system issues was launched earlier this year. The BBC understands it will report this month.

In Freedom of Information responses to the BBC, the Belfast Trust refused to say if the repair costs were being met by relevant building contractors or from taxpayer money.

In a series of questions from the BBC, the trust repeatedly answered: "The trust and its legal representatives continue to engage with independent experts on matters of liability and cannot provide a further update currently."

The new maternity hospital at the Royal Victoria Hospital pictured in 2024

In a statement, Belfast Trust said the current repair cost estimates were in the region of £7m, but the final overall cost for the project is still not known and would also be subject to inflation.

It said the plan to have one part of the new building occupied by March 2027 and the neonatal unit handed over by November 2027 depended on the success of the repair programme.

The Department of Health said it and the Belfast Trust "are reviewing the factors that have led to cost increases and delays".

A DoH statement said the department was "acutely aware of the pressures on public finances".

Adding: "Should specific liability be established, we will ensure that the relevant parties are held accountable."

In a statement, Graham Construction said GBHP successfully handed over the hospital to the trust "in accordance with its contractual obligations".

"Prior to handover, all water quality samples tested within the facility were confirmed to be free from pseudomonas aeruginosa (PsA). These tests were independently witnessed and verified by up to seven separate parties providing robust assurance of compliance at the point of handover," said Graham Construction.

"Following completion of the handover process, GBHP has had no involvement in the management, operation, or maintenance of the hospital. GBHP has not been party to, nor involved in, any matters arising after handover, including the ongoing issues relating to water quality within the building."

The £33m Acute Mental Health facility, on the site of Belfast City Hospital, was opened in 2019 but has also been beset by problems which have forced patients to be relocated .

The repair bill for the facility is £6m, however a further £3.4m has been spent making wards on the Knockbracken Healthcare site in south Belfast suitable to rehouse patients.

Patients are not expected to return to the Acute Mental Health facility until February 2029.

Perezida w’u Burundi, Evariste Ndayishimiye, yashyize umukono ku iteka rivuga ko amatora y’Umukuru w’Igihugu azaba ku wa 3 Gicurasi 2027.

Iryo teka ryo ku wa 4 Ugushyingo 2026, rigaragaza ko amatora y’Umukuru w’Igihugu azaba ku wa 3 Gicurasi 2027. Mu gihe nta mukandida wabona amajwi arenga 50% by’abatoye, hazaba icyiciro cya kabiri cy’amatora azaba ku wa 1 Kamena 2027.

Abifuza kwiyamamariza uyu mwanya bazatanga dosiye zabo muri Komisiyo y’Igihugu y’Amatora , hagati ya tariki ya 13 n’iya 22 Ugushyingo 2026.

Iri teka rinagena ibisabwa ku bakandida bigenga, aho bagomba kuba bamaze nibura umwaka umwe batari mu ishyaka rya politiki. Abigeze kuyobora amashyaka ya politiki bo basabwa kuba bamaze imyaka ibiri bavuye kuri izo nshingano.

Aya matora byemejwe ko Perezida Evariste Ndayishimiye uri ku butegetsi kuva mu 2020 aziyamamaza nk’Umukandinda w’Ishyaka rya CNDD–FDD.

Aya matora yatangiye kuvugwa mu gihe hari amashyaka atavuga rumwe n’ubutegetsi yagaragaje kutishimira uburyo ari gutegurwamo.

Ishyaka Sahwanya-FRODEBU riherutse gutangaza ko ritazatanga umukandida muri aya matora, rivuga ko hari ibyo ritishimiye mu mikorere y’inzego zishinzwe kuyategura.

Iri shyaka rishingira ku byo rivuga ko byaranze amatora yo mu 2025 y’abagize Inteko Ishinga Amategeko, abasenateri, abayobozi b’intara n’abagize inama njyanama z’amakomine. Muri ayo matora, ishyaka CNDD-FDD riri ku butegetsi ryatsinze ku majwi hafi ya yose.

Abandi bamaze kwemeza ko bazaba bashaka intebe iruta izindi mu Biro bya Perezida w’u Burundi, Ntare Rushatsi, barimo Abel Gashatsi wo mu ishyaka UPRONA, Valentin Kavakure wa FPN Imboneza, Gabriel Banzawitonde wa APDR, Francis Rohero wa FPI na Gaspard Kobako wa AND Intadohoka.

British celebrity hairstylist and beauty brand entrepreneur John Frieda has died aged 75.

Frieda became a firm favourite with celebrities throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and is known to have cut hair for clients including British model Twiggy, US First Lady Jackie Kennedy and Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

He was also known for the range of hair products bearing his name, and the iconic Purdey bowl cut which he created for The New Avengers actor Joanna Lumley in 1976.

His death was announced by his hair salon in an Instagram post on Tuesday. , external

"It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully ….surrounded by his family", the statement said

"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.

"Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts."

Throughout his career, Frieda worked with other famous clients including Diana, Princess of Wales, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Scarlett Johansson.

The stylist invented the popular Purdey cut for Joanna Lumley in the 1970s

Frieda was married to Scottish singer Lulu (pictured in 1976) for 14 years

A-list clients at John Frieda's salon included Sex and the City star Sarah Jessica Parker (second right)

Born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951, his father was a hairdresser who owned a salon in Ealing, west London, while his grandfather had also been a Fleet Street barber.

After having gone into the family business, Frieda later joined Leonard Lewis's star-studded salon House of Leonard - famous for having created Twiggy's famous crop - becoming his assistant.

He went on to work for fashion magazines British Vogue and Harper's Bazaar.

In 1976, Frieda opened his own salon in central London which became massively successful and booked up months in advance as his reputation as an influential stylist grew.

He subsequently opened branches across the world, including in Barbados, Ibiza and Los Angeles.

In the 1990s, Frieda stepped back from cutting hair and concentrated on developing his own brand of hair products, including Frizz-Ease hair serum which he created in 1988.

His business empire grew rapidly over the following decade as it expanded into the US and across the world.

In 2002, he and his business partner Gail Federici sold the company to a Japanese conglomerate Kao for $450m (£334m).

Speaking to the British Beauty Council , external in June, Frieda gave his advice for future generation of British hairdressers.

"If you have a client in front of you, rather than thinking about the money or what you're getting from cutting their hair, just think about the action," he said.

"The reward is giving her the best haircut she's ever had. That is your reward."

In 2019, Frieda married Avery Agnelli, with whom he had two children and a step-daughter

Frieda pictured being interviewed in 1991

The stylist photographed with model Lily Cole at Claridges Hotel in 2013

Frieda was married to the singer Lulu from 1977 to 1990 and had one son from that relationship - the actor turned food entrepreneur Jordan Frieda.

He was later married to Avery Agnelli, the widow of Fiat heir Giovanni Agnelli, with whom he had two children and a stepdaughter.

Frieda's step-daughter, Asia Agnelli Lagrange, shared a series of photos of them together down the years on Instagram , external alongside the caption: "Today we lost the best man to ever exist.

"I share this because I know he touched the lives of so many."

Paying tribute, the British Beauty Council sent "love and condolences", while TV presenter and fellow beauty entrepreneur Trinny Woodall commented: "Sending so much love to you all."

Model and TV personality Jo Wood, the ex-wife of Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood, described the news of his death as "so sad".

"When I was 16 and John worked as an assistant at Leonard's he would do my hair," she recalled. "He was so great..."

Cetera Lamb, creative director at Frieda's London salon said the industry had lost "a true legend, a real maverick in hairdressing".

"For 50 years, he led our wonderful salon, leaving behind an incredible legacy of passion, creativity, vision and outstanding hairdressing.

"We will continue in his honour, celebrating his achievements and keeping his memory, values, vision and love for great hairdressing alive. His legacy will live on through us, and we will make sure of that."

MN202611_udumpenj68.t:
Phoebe Waller-Bridge is donating the London flat as part of the Writers' Block scheme

Fleabag creator, writer and actress Phoebe Waller-Bridge is offering a rent-free flat in London for writers early in their careers.

The 41-year-old has bought and donated the flat as part of a new theatre initiative Writers' Block, which aims to address the cost of London accommodation for playwrights from underprivileged backgrounds.

She bought the flat specifically for writers who are starting out and are struggling to afford accommodation in the capital, and has donated its use alongside what the scheme called a "generous financial contribution".

Her flat will be provided without rent, with the resident paying bills only.

Adolescence co-creator Jack Thorne – who wrote the films Wonder and Enola Holmes, as well as the Harry Potter And The Cursed Child stage play – is also providing financial backing to the scheme.

"I was lucky when I started out, my brother lived in Croydon and was able to put me up," he said.

"He did so, rather selflessly, for five years, before I moved to Luton and he got his peace.

"For many writers, the need for a roof makes writing impossible which is why this pilot is so important. If we want stories told about our complicated world, we need writers of every background writing them.

"If you're from privilege, your biggest problem is what to fill a page with. If you're not, so much of your struggle is about the need to survive."

Other backers include playwright and screenwriter James Graham, who wrote stage shows including Ink, Quiz and Dear England, as well as Happy Valley creator Sally Wainwright and The Crown's Peter Morgan.

Waller-Bridge's partner Martin McDonagh is also involved. He is best known for writing and directing films including Oscar and Bafta-winning The Banshees Of Inisherin and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.

Graham said the scheme tackled the class barrier facing writers and helped them avoid "giving up completely".

"The industry's urgent pursuit of representation is still letting down the biggest area of under-representation of all, which is class," he said.

"When I first made it to London, I slept on friends' floors and worked in call centres and bars while I wrote. Every spare room a scheme like this can give to writers starting out in London, not only helps them write but saves them from giving up completely."

Writers' Block was born from the Adopt a Playwright Award initiative, which was founded in 2008 and offers affordable accommodation to writers from disadvantaged backgrounds who need to be in the capital for meetings, rehearsals, performances and career opportunities.

Both schemes were created by Sofie Mason and Diana Jervis-Read.

Umutwe wa politiki n’igisirikare wa Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), uyobowe na Joseph Kabila, watangaje ko utashyigikiye ko manda y’Ingabo z’Umuryango w’Abibumbye ziri mu butumwa bwo kugarura amahoro muri Repubulika Iharanira Demokarasi ya Congo (MONUSCO) yongerwa, uvuga ko ibikorwa byazo mu myaka isaga 28 bitagejeje igihugu ku mutekano urambye.

Ibi byatangajwe ku wa Kabiri, tariki ya 3 Ugushyingo 2026, i Goma, mu Ntara ya Kivu y’Amajyaruguru, nyuma y’inama yahuje Joseph Kabila n’abo bakorana muri FRN, hamwe n’intumwa z’Umuryango w’Abibumbye zari ziyobowe na James Swan, uyobora ubutumwa bwa MONUSCO.

Muri iyo nama, impande zombi zaganiriye ku kongera igihe cy’inshingano za MONUSCO, ziteganyijwe kurangira ku wa 20 Ukuboza 2026. Icyakora, FRN yagaragaje ko itabona impamvu yatuma izo nshingano zongerwa, ahubwo ko iri huriro ryakomeza gahunda yo kuva muri Congo.

Bertrand Bisimwa, Visi Perezida wa FRN, yavuze ko uyu mutwe utanyuzwe n’ibyavuye mu bikorwa bya MONUSCO mu gihe imaze muri Congo, bityo ko kongera manda yayo nta mpinduka zikomeye byazazana ku kibazo cy’umutekano.

Ati “Twaganiriye ku kongera igihe cya manda ya MONUSCO. Ambasaderi Swan ni we wabigarutseho. Air pollution is an annual problem in Delhi and large parts of northern India

Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.

The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.

Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.

Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.

GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.

Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.

Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.

The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.

The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.

Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.

A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.

India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.

The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.

Firecrackers set off during Diwali release particulate matter and gases into the air, adding to the existing pollution

With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.

Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.

Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.

On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.

It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.

The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.

Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.

But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.

In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.

Even Mumbai, India's financial capital, has recorded very high levels of pollution in recent days

It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.

During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.

The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.

On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.

The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.

The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

Prince William thanked the firefighters, military and volunteers who were instrumental in controlling the fire in Treherbert

There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.

Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.

"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.

He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.

Prince William met firefighters who spent the summer tackling blazes

The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.

"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.

"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.

"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) declared a major incident as it was forced to respond to 14 wildfires at the same time in August, including the one above Treherbert.

Support was drafted in from 22 other UK fire services while soldiers were deployed to dig fire breaks and help supply 2.1 million litres of water to douse the flames, including 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment.

Aled Bound, who is crew manager at Maesteg fire station and a retained - on-call - firefighter at Treorchy told Prince William it was "the hardest wildfire season" he and his colleagues had ever dealt with.

Residents were given the order to evacuate as the fire came closer to the village

Months of record-breaking heat and dry conditions sparked a wave of wildfires across the UK through spring and summer.

He described it was "mentally and physically draining".

"I've never had to take so much water up a mountain to put on a fire and still come back the next day because that fire has relit, because it's so deep-seated," Bound said.

With climate change, he warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come".

Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a new all-time high for recorded significant wildfires - 1,350 across England and Wales, up by more than 300 on 2025 and more than 1,000 on 2024.

Aled Bound would have a break after finishing his day job at Maesteg fire station, before racing to Treorchy to fight more fires as an on-call firefighter

Prince William told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer "where I've felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country".

He added: "We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball."

He asked about availability of firefighting aircraft , noting that "the need for aerial assets has been hoisted quite high up in government" as an area "we're lacking".

The prince served a three-year tour flying Sea King helicopters with the Search and Rescue team at RAF Valley on Anglesey between 2010 and 2013, qualifying as a captain.

He recalled flying water bowsers in the Falklands "putting out range fires... and once the Sea King went, we don't have the assets any more".

"I think it's front and centre of many people's minds now, how do we recreate that."

Military helicopters dropped water on fires to ensure they could not return despite the intense heat in the ground - the hillside is still black two months later

Conversation turned to the kit available to fire crews working in unbearable heat, proactive land management practices and whether social media firms could do more to discourage people from setting fires.

Recently, the UK government announced that the RAF's Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft , external would be equipped to fight fires in future.

A separate Welsh government wildfire summit also led to promises of action to improve preparedness , external .

"It feels like this is something we're going to have to live with as a country or as a world now every summer," Prince William said.

Prince William personally thanked firefighters including Adam Openshaw [centre, in firefighting kit] and Aled Bound [to his left]

"It's fair to say that we've learnt a lot from this season... and there's lots that we'll be putting into place, particularly following the wildfire summits," said Adam Openshaw, deputy chief fire officer for SWFRS.

He described the response of people in Treherbert as "the best demonstration of the community coming together to support the wildfire response".

He said it really helped as fire crews worked "tirelessly" in "challenging circumstances".

The fire at Treherbert was considered small but high risk due to its proximity to properties, the difficult terrain and the likelihood of its spreading

Edwards explained that volunteers kept the community centre open 24 hours a day from the Saturday evening of the fire until the following Thursday "to provide whatever service we could".

Due to the unprecedented nature of the fire, the centre became a control hub for the firefighting operation, a place to rest and regroup and a focal point for people wanting to show their support.

Businesses donated food - "40 pizzas arrived within the first 20 minutes" - and there were regular visits from an ice cream van.

Prince William asked whether volunteers should be used more in future and was told the community's efforts, hand in hand with military support, enabled the fire service to focus on bringing the incident under control.

Staff at the Penyrenglyn community centre including Kath Edwards [left] kept the centre open 24/7 for six successive days

"From something really quite horrific, the valleys did what the valleys do very, very well - we pulled together to make a difference," Edwards said.

Communities in the south Wales valleys were already experiencing the effects of climate change, she warned.

"We've had floods, fires... we've got [coal] tips that move as well.

"I think the message I was keen to get across is... we are motivated as a community to ask how do we solve this?

"How can we work together as a community and voluntary sector to support agencies [like the fire service]?"

'I'm not a quitter': Kim Kardashian on retaking the bar exam

It was meant to be Kim Kardashian's triumphant debut as a leading actor - but last year's legal drama All's Fair was so universally panned by critics that it actually broke streaming records as audiences clambered to see what all the fuss was about.

Kardashian, who is best known as a media personality and businesswoman, tells the BBC she had no choice but to "lean into" the discourse and come back for a second series.

"We thought we were this law show, dealing with some really serious issues," she jokes.

But viewers mostly enjoyed its comedy value - with outlandish outfits and zingy one-liners from co-stars Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close sending the show straight into the pantheon of 'camp classics'.

Kim Kardashian has returned to her role as Allura Grant in Ryan Murphy's legal drama All's Fair

"We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.

Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.

The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand .

Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?

"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"

Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.

"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.

Kardashian's co-stars Sarah Paulson and Naomi Watts have also returned for season two

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life , after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.

Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.

"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."

But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice , external , she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.

"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.

"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.

All's Fair was criticised in its first series for bad acting, but Kardashian's co-stars say she has stepped up in the next iteration of the show

Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.

As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".

"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."

One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".

"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins says this year has been "our hardest" yet

Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.

In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.

The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.

It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.

The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.

"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."

The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.

Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.

Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.

"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.

Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.

The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.
